newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - WOLTERS SHARES DIP AFTER RESULTS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - WOLTERS SHARES DIP AFTER RESULTS.

text.p: Dutch business publisher Wolters Kluwer NV reported a 21 percent increase in net profit for the first half of 1997 on Tuesday in line with analysts' forecasts.
But the company's shares dipped 5.70 guilders or two percent to 277.30, partially reversing a gain of 10.10 guilders posted on the eve of the results on Monday.
First-half sales rose 20 percent to 2.42 billion guilders while net profit rose 21 percent to 244 million. Analysts had expected a net profit of around 245 million guilders.
Cash flow from operations, viewed by many analysts as a better gauge of the company's performance, rose 55 percent to 554 million guilders.
The company said it expected earnings per share to rise some 19.5 percent in 1997 to 8.40 guilders and by at least 15 percent a year up to and including 1999.
Wolters Kluwer operates in 25 countries with core activities in legal, tax, business, medical and science publishing. Some 30 percent of sales and profit are generated in the United States.
"Measured in local currencies, nearly all countries contributed to the growth in sales and results," the company said in a statement.
Acquisitions and currency effects, particularly the stronger dollar, helped to fuel the growth of sales and profits.
A company spokeswoman said acquisitions had raised sales by some 10 percent, while currency translation effects had boosted sales by some five percent.
However, not all of the rise in the dollar versus the guilder translates directly into higher profits as the company has substantial amounts of dollar-denominated debt.
Financing charges rose 24 percent in the first half of this year to 102 million guilders, due to the dollar's appreciation and ongoing acquisitions.
Wolters Kluwer said it was particularly pleased with the performance of its U.S. subsidiaries, adding that restructuring of U.S. tax publisher CCH, acquired in 1996, was going to plan.

In Europe, adjustments of the group's Swedish educational publishing business were starting to bear fruit while results in France were boosted by the integration of legal, transport and pharmacology publisher Groupe Liaisons, acquired in late 1996.
Subsidiaries in the Asia-Pacific region, including recently acquired New Zealand based medical publisher Adis, had fully met management's expectations, the company said.
Wolters Kluwer said it would continue to develop electronic media, but added that in many cases such products would complement traditional print products rather than replace them.
"Electronic products are generally not stand-alone. They are usually part of a package of integrated electronic and print information," it said.

Wolters Kluwer and its sector rival Elsevier -- part of the Anglo-Dutch Reed Elsevier group -- have a long track record of outperformance on the Amsterdam stock exchange, fuelled by steady double-digit earnings growth.

Both companies have been laggards during a powerful rally in Dutch share prices so far this year, however most analysts believe they will eventually restore their reputation for generating above-average returns for investors.
"I expect them to start outperforming again sooner or later," said analyst Oskar Tijs of Bangert Pontier.
Tijs said that at current share prices Elsevier seemed to offer better value, but he rated both stocks a Buy.
